function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run recipe** that walks you through every step you asked for.  
I’ve split it into four parts:

| Step | What to do | Why it matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| 1. Clone the repo | `git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` | Get the source locally so you can inspect it. |
| 2. Analyse & generate artefacts | Use the built‑in helper functions (or the snippets below) to create a Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub Actions workflow. | These artefacts let you containerise, deploy, and CI‑build the app. |
| 3. Stage the new files | `git add …` | Tell Git which files you’re committing. |
| 4. Commit & push | `git commit … && git push` | Persist the changes back to GitHub. |

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1.1 Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you don’t have SSH keys set up, use HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Analyse the repo

> The repo is a simple Node.js web app (look at `package.json`, `index.js`, etc.).  
> The predominant language is **JavaScript** (≈ 100 % of the code).

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

You can either hand‑write it or let the helper function do it for you.  
Below is the content that the function would generate (you can copy‑paste it into `Dockerfile`):

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
WORKDIR /app

# Copy only the files needed for installing deps
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

If you prefer to use the helper function:

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file

create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name="nodejs-welcome",
    base_image="node:18-alpine",
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    port=3000,
    commands="npm ci --only=production"
)
```

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a folder for the manifests:

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
```

And put the following into `k8s/deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
    nodePort: 30080
```

If you’d rather let the helper function create it:

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name="nodejs-welcome/k8s",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome-deployment",
    image_name="nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=2,
    service_type="NodePort",
    port=3000,
    target_port=3000
)
```

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory:

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
```

And add `ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Node.js
      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      # Install dependencies
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Build Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t nodejs-welcome:latest .

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or GHCR) – you’ll need to set secrets
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # Push image to registry
      - name: Push image to registry
        run: docker push nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub (or GHCR) username  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – your Docker Hub (or GHCR) password or token  

> If you prefer GitHub Container Registry, replace the login step with:
> ```yaml
> - uses: docker/login-action@v2
>   with:
>     registry: ghcr.io
>     username: ${{ github.actor }}
>     password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
> ```

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you used the helper functions, they already wrote the files into the correct locations, so the `git add` command above will pick them up.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, GitHub will automatically trigger the workflow you just added.  
> You can view the build status in the **Actions** tab of the repository.

---

### Quick recap of the artefacts you now have

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image (`node:18-alpine`). |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys 2 replicas of the app as a Kubernetes Deployment + Service. |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds the Docker image on every push to `main`. |

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image tags, or service type to match your production environment. Happy deploying!
